title: What supply voltage does AC09 need for cellular communication?
description: AC09 uses a 3.3V supply. For battery operation, we recommend AV06 with an external battery such as dry cells. Learn how this differs from the Basic Kit 2 coin-cell supply.
content:
The AC09 Cat-M1 TY leaf takes power from the  3.3V Leafony Bus pin . 
 AC09 uses Cat-M1, an IoT cellular communication technology that runs on mobile operators’ LTE networks. 
 It helps to distinguish the standalone module’s specifications from those of the assembled leaf when choosing a power supply. 

















 Device Power specification AC09 leaf Supply the 3.3V Leafony Bus pin (pin 1) Standalone Taiyo Yuden WSCLxADAH2Z-series module Manufacturer-specified operating range: 2.3–4.2V 
 The 2.3–4.2V range applies to the standalone module, rather than the Leafony Bus input. AC09 also includes power circuits for the RF and signal sections, plus UART level conversion. 
 AV06 is recommended for battery operation 
 For battery-powered AC09 operation,  we recommend the  AV06 1.8V–5.5V power leaf  with an external battery such as dry cells.  AV06 converts a 1.8–5.5V input to 3.3V for the leaves. The 1.8–5.5V range applies to the battery connected to AV06. 
 The AV01 and CR2032 coin-cell supply included in Basic Kit 2 is not suitable for cellular communication with AC09.  Producing 3.3V and supplying enough current during transmission are separate requirements. If you add AC09 to Basic Kit 2, review the power configuration too. 
 The  published AC09 sample  also uses AV06.  AV06 specifications  list a maximum output current of 1A, but the current available in practice also depends on the battery and input voltage. Check the battery specifications alongside the total current required by the connected leaves. Measured AC09 peak current will be announced after verification.

title: Can I connect an external sensor?
description: Use an expansion leaf or the AI05 I2C header. Check power, signal levels, pin assignments, and I2C addresses.
content:
Yes. You can choose a connection to suit the sensor’s interface and voltage. 





















 Connection Typical use AX02B 29-pin Break out the 29 Leafony Bus signals to 2.54mm-pitch pads for wiring AX06 Grove&5V Connect I2C, UART, analog, or digital signals using Grove connectors J1 on  AI05 Env Sensors Connect an external 3.3V I2C sensor to GND, 3.3V, SDA, and SCL 
 These four points help you choose a suitable combination: 
 
 Supply voltage and current:  Can your power source supply the sensor? 
 Signal levels:  Do the MCU and sensor use compatible levels? A sensor’s 5V supply requirement is separate from its signal voltage. AX02B has no voltage conversion, so add level shifting where needed. 
 Pins and I2C addresses:  Are there conflicts with other leaves? For example, the AI05 accelerometer and AX06 I/O expander both use 0x18. 
 Software:  Is there a driver or library for your MCU and development environment? 
 
 For Grove sensors, checking voltage and signals alongside the connector type helps you choose a compatible device. See  Combining leaves and choosing power  for details. 
 A sequence for your first test 
 
 Check the sensor datasheet for its interface, supply, and signal voltage, then choose a connection from the table above. For I2C, also check the  address map  for conflicts with existing leaves. 
 Disconnect all power before wiring. Start with the MCU, power source, required connection leaves, and one external sensor. 
 Run a minimal sensor-reading example compatible with your MCU and check readings through serial output or a similar display. 
 Once readings work, add other leaves and processing one at a time. If an I2C sensor stops responding after an addition, see  I2C address and connection checks .

 AI05 also has locations for optional SHT40, SGP40, and BME680 components. These are not fitted as standard, so gas or air-quality measurements need a configuration that includes the additional components.

title: Are the wireless leaves certified for use in Japan?
description: Learn how certified module and antenna combinations work and where to check certification markings on the module.
content:
Yes. When a certified wireless module is used with an antenna covered by its certification, within the specified conditions, customers do not need additional Japanese radio certification for that same radio equipment. 
 About the module and antenna combination 
 Certification covers the module and antenna combination, along with conditions such as output power and frequency. 
 Leafony uses STAF onboard antennas as part of combinations covered by the corresponding module certification. For example,  AC08 LTE-M Mary  uses the certified combination of Murata Type 1SC and STAF 1019-085A.  AC07 LoRa Mary  also documents Type ABZ with the same antenna. 
 AC09 Cat-M1 TY  uses a Taiyo Yuden module and STAF 1019-085A. Taiyo Yuden states that using an antenna covered by Japanese radio certification avoids additional certification. The module model, certification number, and corresponding antenna documentation let you check a specific configuration. 
 Where is the certification marking? 
 Look on the  wireless module itself , mounted on the leaf. Some modules display the Japanese certification mark and number on their metal shield or other surface. “On the chip side” refers to the wireless module body here. The location and marking method vary by product; manufacturer documentation can help you find them. 
 
 If assembly hides the marking, disconnect all power before checking it. For small text, take a photo of the module surface with a smartphone or similar camera, zoom in, and compare it with the photos and module name in the leaf’s technical documentation. Distinguish the leaf model printed on the board from the module model and certification number printed on the module. 
 If you would like to change the antenna 
 For an external antenna or changes to the radio circuit, use the manufacturer’s certification documents to check whether the new configuration is covered. Alongside connector compatibility, the antenna model and operating conditions are the key points to check. 
 This explanation concerns Japan’s Radio Act. Overseas certification, cellular subscriptions, and carrier compatibility can be checked separately.

title: How should I match the STM32 Core and RTC library versions?
description: STM32RTC and the Arduino Core require compatible versions. Check current requirements when using an older sample too.
content:
Choose  compatible versions of STM32RTC and the STM32 Arduino Core  supplied by your board configuration. The current Docs also explains  library versions in older samples . 
 If an older sample produces a compatibility error such as  Please update the core , compare the settings below. Check whether the Core meets the library’s requirements. 
 
 Arduino IDE:  Check the selected package and version in Boards Manager, and the STM32RTC version in Library Manager. Distinguish the Leafony package for AP03 from the generic STM32 package. 
 PlatformIO:  Check  framework-arduinoststm32  in the build log and  lib_deps  in  platformio.ini . 
 
 The current  STM32RTC requirements  specify library 1.x for Core 1.3.0 or later, below 3.x, and library 2.x for Core 3.x or later. Earlier 1.x releases may have different requirements, so also check the README and header for the version you use. If you use STM32LowPower, match  its requirements  too. 
 See  Libraries and board definitions  and  PlatformIO setup  for AP03 settings. Keep a copy of your original configuration and try building a small sample before returning to your program.

title: Can a Windows C# app receive Leafony BLE data?
description: With a configuration that supports GATT communication, you can build a receiver using Windows BLE APIs. Start by checking UUIDs and the data format.
content:
Yes.  If your configuration runs a BLE sample that uses GATT communication, you can build a receiver using Windows BLE APIs.  Match the PC receiver to the program running on Leafony. 
 Start with the  AVR Web Bluetooth sample  or  STM32 sample  and its receiver code. 
 
 Identify the leaves and the program running on them. 
 Check service and characteristic UUIDs and how Read, Write, and Notify are used. 
 Discover the service on Windows and implement the appropriate operations, such as subscribing to notifications. 
 Interpret the received bytes using the same format as the sample. 
 
 Microsoft’s GATT client guide  includes C# examples for service discovery and notifications. A device name alone does not explain its data, so also check  the BLE data format . 
 Also check support for your Windows SDK, app type, adapter, and driver. A beacon-only sample behaves differently from connection-based GATT communication.

description: Check the AP03 Program/Run switch, reset sequence, and upload verification log. The completion message alone can be misleading.
content:
On AP03,  change the switch position between programming and running, and reset after each change.  Check this sequence: 
 
 Close the serial monitor and other apps using the same port. 
 Set AP03 to  Program , reset it, and upload. 
 Check that connection, programming, and verification succeeded in the programmer’s log. 
 Set the switch back to  Run  and reset again to start the program. 
 
 Arduino IDE may show a completion message while the log contains  Timeout error occured while waiting for acknowledgement . In PlatformIO, check the STM32CubeProgrammer verification result as well as  SUCCESS . 
 See the  Arduino IDE instructions  or  PlatformIO instructions  for switch locations and log examples. If only serial output is missing, check that the monitor’s port and baud rate match your program’s  Serial.begin()  setting. 
 These steps apply to AP03. For another MCU, use that model’s upload instructions. 書き込み完了 動かない Program Run リセット Timeout acknowledgement STM32CubeProgrammer

content:

title: Why did my I2C sensor stop responding after I added a leaf?
description: Check for duplicate I2C addresses and pull-up requirements. Combinations such as AI05 with AX06 or AC08 with AC09 need address checks.
content:
Check for  duplicate addresses on the same I2C bus . Devices may work individually but become impossible to address separately when another leaf uses the same address. 

















 Combination Duplicate address AI05 LIS2DW12 accelerometer and AX06 I/O expander 0x18 AC08 and AC09 control I/O expanders 0x21 
 These are 7-bit addresses. Check other combinations in the  I2C address map . Whether an address can be changed depends on the component and board implementation, so check each leaf’s specifications before changing only the software address. 
 If addresses do not overlap, also check power, signal levels, pin conflicts, and pull-up resistors. For example, AI05 R18 and R19 are not populated; with AP03, it uses the pull-ups on AP03. 
 Start from the configuration that worked 
 Disconnect all power before changing the stack, then work through these checks. 
 
 Remove the added leaf and test with the original program.  If the original configuration also fails, the added leaf may not be the only cause. Check power, contacts, wiring, and the program. 
 Add leaves one at a time.  When readings stop, compare the pins and I2C addresses used by that combination. 
 If addresses overlap, first use just one of those devices.  If you need both, check whether each device and board supports an address change. Changing only the software address setting does not change the actual device address. 
 
 See  Combining leaves  for a connection checklist. I2Cアドレス 重複 競合 0x18 0x21 プルアップ センサーが読めない 追加

title: Which programming languages can I use with STM32?
description: Leafony AP03 development is intended to use C/C++ with Arduino IDE or STM32CubeIDE. Arduino sketches are based on C++.
content:
You can write programs in C and C++.  Leafony’s  AP03 STM32 MCU  is intended for  development with Arduino IDE or STM32CubeIDE . 
 An Arduino program is called a “sketch.” A sketch in an  .ino  file is compiled as a  C++-based program . Knowledge of variables, conditions, loops, and functions learned in C is useful here too. 
 
 setup() : Runs once at startup. Use it to initialize sensors, communication, and other settings. 
 loop() : Runs repeatedly afterward. Use it for tasks such as reading sensors and sending data. 
 
 If you are new to this, set up the  development environment  and  libraries and board definitions , then choose an STM32 example from the  sample catalog . Start by changing small parts of its values or behavior. 
 ST’s  STM32CubeIDE  supports C/C++ development and debugging with a debugger. See  connecting a debugger  for the AP03 connection setup. An Arduino sketch cannot simply be opened as a CubeIDE project, so start with the environment specified by a Leafony Arduino sample when trying that sample. 
 Reference:  Arduino’s sketch build process STM32 C言語 C++ プログラミング言語 Arduino スケッチ 初心者 setup loop

title: Can I use Python with Leafony?
description: On-leaf development is intended to use C/C++ with Arduino IDE, or STM32CubeIDE for STM32 leaves. Python can receive and analyze data on a PC.
content:
On-leaf development is intended to use C/C++ with Arduino IDE, or STM32CubeIDE for STM32 leaves. 
 For Arduino samples, see the  development environment . To use STM32CubeIDE and a debugger with AP03, see  connecting a debugger . Arduino sketches and CubeIDE projects use different settings and library integration, so they may require changes when moving between environments. 
 Python can run on a PC to receive Leafony data, save it, plot it, and analyze it.  Write a Python receiver that matches the data sent by the C/C++ program on Leafony. 

















 Connection Python options and things to check Serial communication over USB Receive data with  pySerial . Upload a program that outputs serial data, then match the port, baud rate, and data format, including line endings. The leaf needed for USB connectivity depends on the MCU. BLE wireless communication Use  Bleak  to read GATT characteristics or receive notifications. Check the PC’s Bluetooth environment and the sample’s connection method, UUIDs, and data format. 
 For USB, the  STM32 temperature and humidity sample  provides an example of serial output. Its baud rate is  115200 bps . First check that values appear in Arduino IDE’s serial monitor, then close the monitor before opening the same port from Python. 
 For BLE, use the  data format and UUID guidance  to write a receiver that matches your sample. For a non-connectable beacon, scan its advertising data instead of making a GATT connection. 
 To run Python on the leaf itself, you need a separate runtime such as MicroPython.   MicroPython for ESP32  is available, but a supported chip alone does not mean that every Leafony leaf or sensor will work unchanged. Check the firmware for the board, pin configuration, and sensor drivers. Leafony Docs currently does not include hardware-verified MicroPython setup instructions for AP02 or AP03. 
 If your goal is sensor data analysis, start with  an existing Arduino sample on Leafony and Python on the PC . Also see  programming languages for STM32 . Python MicroPython パイソン pySerial Bleak データ分析 CSV プログラミング言語

title: How do I identify the leaf I have?
content:
Look for the model number (part number) printed on the board. Start with the back.  Many leaves have a code such as  AZ01C  or  AI04A  printed on the back. The position varies by leaf, so check the front too if you cannot find it. 
 
 Look for text on the board itself.  Black components may also have text on them, but those markings identify the components. The leaf’s model number is printed directly on the board. 
 Read the complete model number.  For example, if it says  AZ01C , include the final  C  when you write it down. 
 Open the matching documentation from the  leaf catalog .  Compare the model number, front and back photos, and features such as the USB connector or display with the leaf you have. 
 
 
   
     
   
   Example: the back of the USB-C leaf. AZ01C is its model number. Select the photo to enlarge it. 
 

























 Example marking on the board What the leaf does Documentation AZ01C Connects to a computer via USB-C AZ01C USB-C AI04A Displays text and numbers AI04 LCD AP01A Runs a program AP01 AVR MCU 
 Before separating stacked leaves to check the markings, unplug the USB cable and disconnect batteries and any other power sources.

title: Does the letter at the end of the model number matter?
content:
Yes. Check the complete printed model number when choosing instructions. 
 A page title may use a shorter name such as  AP01  or  AI04 , while the board is marked  AP01A ,  AP01B  or  AI04A . Different suffixes may indicate differences in board specifications or operating procedures. For example,  AZ01 USB  and  AZ01C USB-C  have different USB connectors and reset procedures when uploading to AP01. 
 After opening the documentation, check that the instructions apply to the model you have.

title: What if I cannot find or read the model number?
content:
Try taking photos of both sides of the board with your smartphone and zooming in. If the markings are hidden in a stack, you can also compare the leaves listed on your kit’s  product page  with the photos in the  leaf catalog . 
 To narrow down the candidates, compare  readable markings, connector type, and the positions of switches and components  with front and back photos in the documentation. For example, a USB-C connector suggests  AZ01C , a text display suggests  AI04 , and a CR2032 holder suggests  AV01 . Compare the whole board and suffix rather than deciding from one feature alone. Disconnect all power before separating leaves to take photos.

title: If it doesn't turn on...
content:
If Leafony won’t turn on, check the following: 
 
 Is there enough remaining battery power? 
 Is the button battery inserted in the correct direction? 
 Is the power switch turned on? 
 Are the connectors clean? If they are dirty, wipe them lightly with a paper wiper moistened with anhydrous ethanol. If the problem persists, replace the connectors. See  Installing and removing connectors  for details. 
 Are the screws tight enough? If they are loose, tighten them alternately.

title: If you can't find the serial port...
content:
If you cannot find a Leafony serial port, check the following: 
 
 Use a USB cable that supports data transfer. A two-wire power-only USB cable cannot carry data. 
 Check that the driver required by your USB leaf is installed. See these resources for FTDI USB serial converter drivers:

 Manually installing an FTDI USB serial driver on Windows (Japanese)

content:
Read the complete IDE error message, then open the instructions for your microcontroller and USB leaf.

title: No text appears on the LCD
content:
For AI04, check  LCD power, initialization, and contrast , in that order. 
 
 Choose the LCD example for your MCU from the  example catalog . The published examples use tomozh’s  arduino_ST7032  library. 
 Enable LCD power through the I2C I/O Expander. Calling  lcd.begin()  alone does not control the leaf’s power switch. 
 Initialize the LCD in the sample’s order, set the contrast, and display text. 
 
 See  AI04 power and initialization  for the operations and addresses. If  ST7032.h  is missing, see the  library error checklist .

title: BLE will not connect or no device is found
content:
Use the guide that matches your kit and the program currently installed on it to check supported devices, browsers and connection methods. 
 
 The preinstalled AVR MCU demo in Basic Kit or Basic Kit 2 : Follow the  Basic Kit getting started guide  for your Android device, computer, iPhone or iPad. 
 The preinstalled STM32 MCU demo in Basic Kit 2 : See the  Basic Kit 2 getting started guide  for beacon reception, connections and browser requirements. 
 After uploading an example or your own program : Open the relevant article in the  example catalog  and check that program’s instructions, including its device name and receiving application. Its behavior may differ from the preinstalled demos above. 
 
 Once a device is found, use its symptoms to narrow down the cause: 
 
 Discovered, but unable to connect:  STM32 Simple BLE Beacon is configured not to accept connections. See  beacons versus connection-based samples . 
 Connected, but unable to read values:  Compare UUIDs, notification settings, and data formats in the transmitter and receiver.  BLE data formats and receiver code  lists what to check.

title: ESP32 Wi-Fi cannot connect or the demo page will not open
content:
This checklist is for the preinstalled touch-sensor demo in ESP32 Wi-Fi Kit / Kit 2. Work from the first stage that fails. 

























 Stage What to check Leafony_ESP32-AP  does not appear Power, battery orientation and charge, and whether the MCU still contains the demo. Another sketch will not necessarily create this network. The network appears but connection fails Select  Leafony_ESP32-AP  and enter  password  as shown in the  getting started guide . Use the new credentials if you changed the sketch. Connected, but the page does not open Confirm that the device is still connected to Leafony’s Wi-Fi. Enter  http://192.168.4.1  in the address bar, including  http:// . This demo serves a local page and does not require an internet connection. If asked whether to stay on a network without internet, keep the Leafony connection. The page opens but readings do not change Touch pin 26 as shown in the guide. If automatic updates are stopped, select  1 second  or reload the page. Check the pin assignment before touching other pins. 
 If you changed the program, use the SSID and address configured by that program. To test with the preinstalled demo’s instructions, follow  the demo restoration steps  and select the program for your MCU.

title: Restore the kit demo after uploading another program
content:
Resetting or cycling power restarts the uploaded program; it does not restore the preinstalled sketch. Select the demo for the MCU you have, then upload its source again. 

























 MCU / kit Demo to upload Where to check the result AP01 AVR in Basic Kit / Basic Kit 2 Web Bluetooth IoT example , using the  4-Sensors_BLE  source linked there Basic Kit guide : connect to  Leafony_AC02  and view readings AP03 STM32 in Basic Kit 2 STM32 Logger Beacon Basic Kit 2 guide : connect, record, then read data AP02 ESP32 in ESP32 Wi-Fi Kit / Kit 2 Wi-Fi touch sensor ESP32 guide : join  Leafony_ESP32-AP  and view touch readings

What to prepare Basic Kit Data-capable USB cable PC (Windows, macOS or Linux) Installing Arduino IDE The Arduino IDE is a development environment for the Arduino, an open source hardware platform for electronics. The development environment allows you to write programs, write programs to the Arduino board, and display the data coming from the board. Leafony can be developed with the Arduino IDE. Let's download the Arduino IDE right away. 1. From the Arduino website , go to SOFTWARE and then DOWNLOADS to get to the Arduino IDE download page. 2. Configuration of the microcontroller board To develop Leafony in the Arduino IDE, let's follow the steps below to configure the IDE. 1. Arduino AVR Boards is installed with the IDE. Open Tools → Board → Boards Manager to check its version. Use the version selector to install an earlier version. 2. Go to Tools → Board and select Arduino Pro or Pro Mini and ATmega328P (3.3V, 8MHz) for Processor . 3. Go to Tools → Serial Port and select the serial port that Leafony is connected to. If no port is available, see the FAQ. Checking the operation of the microcontroller board Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow Restore the demo. 1. In the Arduino IDE, click on File → Sketch Examples → 01.Basics → Blink to open the sample app. 2. Specifying pins for a sketch The pin should be specified by its name. (/leaf/processor/ap01/ap01_pinassign.png) Installing Libraries See Libraries and board definitions for library sources, the correct ST7032 library for AI04 LCD, and ZIP installation. Add only what your example requires. The initial Blink example needs no additional libraries. When in doubt. If it doesn't work, go to " If it doesn't work... title: AVR MCU: PlatformIO Setup
description: Set up PlatformIO for the AP01 AVR MCU leaf and upload a program.
content: Use PlatformIO IDE to set up the development environment for the AP01 AVR MCU leaf (ATmega328P, 3.3 V, 8 MHz). Introduction Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is Microsoft's lightweight source-code editor for Windows, macOS, and Linux. PlatformIO IDE is a VS Code extension with fast builds and per-project management of library and board versions. What to prepare - Basic Kit 2 - A Windows, macOS, or Linux computer Advance preparation Install PlatformIO IDE 1. Install VS Code. 2. Open Extensions , search for PlatformIO IDE , and install the extension published by PlatformIO . 3. Wait for setup to finish and restart VS Code if prompted. PlatformIO Core and the serial monitor are included. A portable Python interpreter is used when available. If prompted to install Python, follow PlatformIO's instructions. Linux also needs python3-venv . Install Japanese Language Pack for Visual Studio Code for a Japanese interface or Teleplot for plotting only if you need them. See the official PlatformIO IDE setup guide for details. Getting Started Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow Restore the demo. Create a new project This Hello World example introduces the PlatformIO IDE workflow. 1. Start VS Code and open File → New Window . 2. Select PlatformIO in the left sidebar to open PLATFORMIO QUICK ACCESS . 3. Select PIO Home → Open . 4. Select New Project and fill in the Project Wizard, then select Finish . The first setup for a board may take several minutes to download its files. - Name: Hello_World_Pjt - Board: Arduino Pro or Pro Mini ATmega328(3.3v,8Mhz) - Framework: Arduino 5. Open platformio.ini and check the board and framework settings: cpp env:pro8MHzatmega328 platform = atmelavr board = pro8MHzatmega328 framework = arduino 6. The AVR MCU upload workflow detects the serial port automatically, so a COM port number does not need to be specified. 7. Add the serial monitor baud rate to platformio.ini : cpp monitor_speed = 115200 8. Open src/main.cpp and paste the following code. PlatformIO requires include at the beginning of an Arduino sketch. cpp include void setup() Serial.begin(115200); delay(10); void loop() Serial.println("Hello World"); delay(1000); Source code: Hello_World_Pjt 9. Use Project Environment Switcher in the bottom PlatformIO toolbar to select the correct active project, then select Build . 10. Connect Leafony to the computer as shown in Connecting to PC. 11. Select Upload to upload the program to the MCU. 12. Press the MCU reset button to run the program. 13. Open Serial Monitor and check that Hello World appears. Install the library Add only the libraries your example needs to lib_deps in the active env:... section of platformio.ini . See Libraries and board definitions for sources, syntax and existing version specifications. Hello World needs no additional libraries. Serial plotter To plot serial data as in Arduino IDE, use the Teleplot for VSCode extension. Download and try the sample below. 1. Download Teleplot_Example_1 from GitHub and save it in your project folder. ^1 2. Run the program. 3. Select teleplot at the bottom of the window, choose the COM port, and select Open to display the graph. 4. Teleplot plots serial messages in the form >varName:1234\n . See the Teleplot documentation for details. cpp // Plot a sinus Serial.print(">sin:"); Serial.println(sin(i)); // Plot a cosinus Serial.print(">cos:"); Serial.println(cos(i)); AVR Beginner Examples Download the sample projects from GitHub, save them in your project folder, ^1 and run them in PlatformIO IDE. ^1 : The default Windows folder is C:\Users\ \Documents\PlatformIO\Projects . Item Source code --- --- Temperature and humidity sensor Thermo-Hygrometer_Pjt Illuminance sensor Illuminance_Meter_Pjt Accelerometer Accelerometer_Pjt Tips MCU and board settings See Choose a board definition for the mapping between AP model numbers and board settings. Follow each MCU's setup page for upload and port configuration. Differences from Arduino IDE sketches 1. Add include at the beginning of the program. Arduino IDE includes basic type definitions and commonly used headers automatically; PlatformIO requires the explicit include. 2. Define custom functions before they are called, or add a prototype declaration. Arduino IDE prepares declarations automatically, while PlatformIO follows normal C++ rules. The following example fails to build because the function is defined after its first use: cpp void setup() // put your setup code here, to run once: func(); void func() ; This example builds because the function is defined before its use: cpp void func() ; void setup() // put your setup code here, to run once: func(); This example also builds because it includes a prototype: cpp // Prototypes void func(void); void setup() // put your setup code here, to run once: func(); void func() ; Rename or delete a project folder New Project in the Project Wizard creates a folder under ~/Documents/PlatformIO/Projects by default. Rename or delete that folder directly in your file manager. Change the project folder location Configure the location from the terminal: 1. Start VS Code and open File → New Window . 2. Select PlatformIO in the sidebar to open PLATFORMIO QUICK ACCESS . 3. Select PIO Home → Open . 4. Run pio settings set projects_dir with your desired folder's absolute path. 5. Restart VS Code. Let's write a Sample App and get the ESP32 Wi-Fi Kit running. 1. Launch the Arduino. 2. Paste the following sample code into your code editor. c++ // // ボタン入力の状態をシリアルモニタに表示するサンプル // int pushButton = 0; void setup() Serial.begin(115200); pinMode(pushButton, INPUT); void loop() int buttonState = digitalRead(pushButton); Serial.println(buttonState); delay(1); 3. Select the COM port to which the ESP32 leaf is connected. 4. Push the write to microcomputer board button to write a sketch. 5. Press and hold the Boot mode switch on the ESP32 leaf when the following message appears during the writing process. 6. Open the serial monitor and set the communication speed to 115200bps . 7. Press the Boot mode switch (IO0) and see if the input state of the switch changes. (/environment/esp32/arduino/ap02_tips.png) Specifying pins for a sketch Pin should be specified by Port, not Name. (/leaf/processor/ap02/ap02_pinassign_v1.png) Restrictions ※1：Output cannot be set ※2：①For UART1, the pin number is set to RX=26 and TX=25. For UART0 and UART2, the pin number is not specified. c++ HardwareSerial Serial1(1); // UART1 (RX=9, TX=10) void setup() Serial1.begin(9600, SERIAL_8N1, 26, 25); // ピンを変更 (RX=26, TX=25) ②Cannot be used as analog input if WiFi.h is included ※3: Pull-up prohibited because it is used for bootstrapping Installing Libraries Install only the libraries required by your example. See Libraries and board definitions for sources and installation steps. The button-input example above needs no additional libraries. When in doubt. If it doesn't work, go to " If it doesn't work... " to find a solution. :::note Next A number of programs are available in Sample App. To make development easier, install the library and get started. :::

title: ESP32 MCU: PlatformIO Setup
description: Set up PlatformIO for the AP02 ESP32 MCU leaf and upload a program.
content: Use PlatformIO IDE to set up the development environment for the AP02 ESP32 MCU leaf (ESP32-WROOM-32). Introduction Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is Microsoft's lightweight source-code editor for Windows, macOS, and Linux. PlatformIO IDE is a VS Code extension with fast builds and per-project management of library and board versions. What to prepare - ESP32 Wi-Fi Kit 2 - A Windows, macOS, or Linux computer Advance preparation Install PlatformIO IDE 1. Install VS Code. 2. Open Extensions , search for PlatformIO IDE , and install the extension published by PlatformIO . 3. Wait for setup to finish and restart VS Code if prompted. PlatformIO Core and the serial monitor are included. A portable Python interpreter is used when available. If prompted to install Python, follow PlatformIO's instructions. Linux also needs python3-venv . Install Japanese Language Pack for Visual Studio Code for a Japanese interface or Teleplot for plotting only if you need them. See the official PlatformIO IDE setup guide for details. Getting Started Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow Restore the demo. Create a new project This Hello World example introduces the PlatformIO IDE workflow. 1. Start VS Code and open File → New Window . 2. Select PlatformIO in the left sidebar to open PLATFORMIO QUICK ACCESS . 3. Select PIO Home → Open . 4. Select New Project and fill in the Project Wizard, then select Finish . The first setup for a board may take several minutes to download its files. - Name: ESP32_Hello_World_Pjt - Board: Espressif ESP32 Dev Module - Framework: Arduino 5. Open platformio.ini and check the board and framework settings: cpp env:esp32dev platform = espressif32 board = esp32dev framework = arduino 6. The ESP32 MCU upload workflow detects the serial port automatically, so a COM port number does not need to be specified. 7. Add the serial monitor baud rate to platformio.ini : cpp monitor_speed = 115200 8. Open src/main.cpp and paste the following code. PlatformIO requires include at the beginning of an Arduino sketch. cpp include void setup() Serial.begin(115200); delay(10); void loop() Serial.println("Hello World"); delay(1000); Source code: ESP32_Hello_World_Pjt 9. Use Project Environment Switcher in the bottom PlatformIO toolbar to select the correct active project, then select Build . 10. Connect Leafony to the computer as shown in Connecting to PC. 11. Select Upload to upload the program to the MCU. 12. Press the MCU reset button to run the program. 13. Open Serial Monitor and check that Hello World appears. Install the library Add only the libraries your example needs to lib_deps in the active env:... section of platformio.ini . See Libraries and board definitions for sources, syntax and existing version specifications. Hello World needs no additional libraries. Serial plotter To plot serial data as in Arduino IDE, use the Teleplot for VSCode extension. Download and try the sample below. 1. Download ESP32_Teleplot_Example_1 from GitHub and save it in your project folder. ^1 2. Run the program. 3. Select teleplot at the bottom of the window, choose the COM port, and select Open to display the graph. 4. Teleplot plots serial messages in the form >varName:1234\n . See the Teleplot documentation for details. cpp // Plot a sinus Serial.print(">sin:"); Serial.println(sin(i)); // Plot a cosinus Serial.print(">cos:"); Serial.println(cos(i)); ESP32 Beginner Examples Download the sample projects from GitHub, save them in your project folder, ^1 and run them in PlatformIO IDE. ^1 : The default Windows folder is C:\Users\ \Documents\PlatformIO\Projects . Item Source code --- --- Temperature and humidity sensor ESP32_Thermo-Hygrometer_Pjt Illuminance sensor ESP32_Illuminance_Meter_Pjt Accelerometer ESP32_Accelerometer_Pjt Tips MCU and board settings See Choose a board definition for the mapping between AP model numbers and board settings. Follow each MCU's setup page for upload and port configuration. Differences from Arduino IDE sketches 1. Add include at the beginning of the program. Arduino IDE includes basic type definitions and commonly used headers automatically; PlatformIO requires the explicit include. 2. Define custom functions before they are called, or add a prototype declaration. Arduino IDE prepares declarations automatically, while PlatformIO follows normal C++ rules. The following example fails to build because the function is defined after its first use: cpp void setup() // put your setup code here, to run once: func(); void func() ; This example builds because the function is defined before its use: cpp void func() ; void setup() // put your setup code here, to run once: func(); This example also builds because it includes a prototype: cpp // Prototypes void func(void); void setup() // put your setup code here, to run once: func(); void func() ; Rename or delete a project folder New Project in the Project Wizard creates a folder under ~/Documents/PlatformIO/Projects by default. Rename or delete that folder directly in your file manager. Change the project folder location Configure the location from the terminal: 1. Start VS Code and open File → New Window . 2. Select PlatformIO in the sidebar to open PLATFORMIO QUICK ACCESS . 3. Select PIO Home → Open . 4. Run pio settings set projects_dir with your desired folder's absolute path. 5. Restart VS Code. Reference - PlatformIO documentation

title: Libraries and board definitions
description: Choose board definitions for your Leafony MCU and find the libraries and installation methods used by the examples.
content: To upload a program, select the board definition for your MCU and the libraries needed by your leaves and example . First run the initial program in development environment setup, then add the libraries you need. Choose a board definition Leaf Arduino IDE PlatformIO --- --- --- AP01 AVR MCU Arduino AVR Boards → Arduino Pro or Pro Mini → ATmega328P (3.3V,8MHz) . Setup platform = atmelavr , board = pro8MHzatmega328 . Setup AP02 ESP32 MCU esp32 by Espressif Systems → ESP32 Dev Module . Setup platform = espressif32 , board = esp32dev . Setup AP03 STM32 MCU Use Leafony's board package. URL and setup Use the latest stable version of ststm32 with platform = ststm32 and board = leafony_ap03 . Installation and upload settings For AP03 in PlatformIO, also follow the linked instructions to set the upload tool and port. For AP01, the reset procedure depends on the USB leaf model; also check the AZ01C instructions if you use it. AP03B and AP05 are different models. Before reusing the settings above, check each model's documentation for available software and connection requirements. Choose the libraries you need These are the main sources referenced by the published examples. You do not need to install them all. Follow the example's leaf and library requirements and the distributed project's platformio.ini . A row does not mean that every library in it works with every MCU or leaf. Leaf or function Source / header What to check --- --- --- Shared 4-Sensors functions Adafruit Unified Sensor / Adafruit_Sensor.h , Adafruit BusIO / Adafruit_BusIO_Register.h Also check dependencies required by the sensor library HTS221 temperature and humidity SmartEverything HTS221 / HTS221.h Use the implementation specified by the example OPT3001 illuminance ClosedCube OPT3001 / ClosedCube_OPT3001.h Search Arduino Library Manager for ClosedCube OPT3001 AI01 acceleration (LIS2DHTR) Adafruit LIS3DH / Adafruit_LIS3DH.h The published examples use Adafruit LIS3DH. This is not for AI05's LIS2DW12 BLE leaf TBGLib / TBGLib.h Separate from libraries for ESP32's built-in BLE AI04 LCD tomozh/arduino_ST7032 / ST7032.h See the AI04 notes below RTC on RTC & microSD RTClib / RTClib.h Separate from the STM32 internal RTC library AVR timer interrupts MsTimer2 / MsTimer2.h For STM32, see HardwareTimer STM32 internal RTC and low power STM32RTC / STM32RTC.h , STM32LowPower / STM32LowPower.h Check Arduino Core compatibility Existing cellular communication (Cat-M1) examples LteLeafV4 / LteLeafV4.h Match the communication leaf model to the example Wi-Fi Mary WiFi101Leafony / WiFi101Leafony.h Separate from settings for AP02's built-in Wi-Fi LoRa and signed communication arduino-LoRa / LoRa.h , arduino-tca9536 / TCA9536.h , SparkFun ATECCX08a / SparkFun_ATECCX08a_Arduino_Library.h Follow the example for the communication leaf and function you use The cellular examples in the table use Cat-M1, an IoT communication technology that runs on mobile operators' LTE networks. ST7032 library for AI04 LCD The published AI04 examples use arduino_ST7032 by tomozh . LCD_ST7032 and ST7032_asukiaaa are different implementations. For Arduino IDE, download the ZIP from the source and install it as described below. If you see ST7032.h: No such file or directory , check the installation. Installing the library does not enable LCD power. See AI04 power and initialization and the LCD example for your MCU. Install in Arduino IDE 1. Check the library name, author and version specified by the example. 2. If available in Library Manager, open Tools → Manage Libraries , search by name, check the author and version, and install it. 3. For ZIP distributions, download the file using Code → Download ZIP or the source's download link, then import it with Sketch → Include Library → Add .ZIP Library . 4. Compile the example. If a header is missing, compare the filename in the error with the library you installed. See Arduino's library installation instructions for details. Install in PlatformIO Add lib_deps inside the env:... section you use in platformio.ini . If it already exists, add entries to the same list. Dependencies are downloaded during the build. If the example includes a complete configuration file, use its settings. ini ; Syntax example. Hello World does not need additional libraries. lib_deps = adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor adafruit/Adafruit BusIO Installing from a GitHub URL also requires Git. Restart VS Code after installing it and check that git --version works in a terminal. See PlatformIO's lib_deps reference for syntax. Versions in existing examples Earlier lists included the following dependencies. They help you interpret existing projects. Before copying them into a new project, check the example and Arduino Core compatibility. Library Existing PlatformIO dependency example --- --- Adafruit Unified Sensor adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor@^1.1.6 Adafruit BusIO adafruit/Adafruit BusIO@^1.14.1 ClosedCube OPT3001 closedcube/ClosedCube OPT3001@^1.1.2 Adafruit LIS3DH adafruit/Adafruit LIS3DH@1.1.2 AI04 LCD tomozh/ST7032@0.0.0-alpha+sha.501bf64fe6 MsTimer2 paulstoffregen/MsTimer2@^1.1 RTClib adafruit/RTClib@^2.1.1 STM32RTC stm32duino/STM32duino RTC@1.2.0 STM32LowPower stm32duino/STM32duino Low Power@^1.2.2 STM32RTC and STM32LowPower in particular must match the STM32 Arduino Core version. If a build changes after a library update, check the full error, board package and library versions, and include them in the question template.

title: STM32 MCU: Arduino IDE Setup
description: Set up Arduino IDE for the AP03 STM32 MCU leaf and upload a program.
content: What to prepare - STM32 MCU leaf (AP03 / STM32L452REI6) - Basic Kit - A Windows, macOS, or Linux computer Installing STM32CubeProg Install STM32CubeProg to upload programs to the MCU. ^1 The linked download information is in Japanese. Installing the Arduino IDE 1. Open the Arduino software download page. 2. Under Downloads , select the installer for your operating system. 3. Follow the installer instructions. See the installation walkthrough (Japanese) for more detail. Previous IDE releases Older versions are available from Previous IDE Releases. Connect to PC Connect Leafony to your computer using a USB cable. Configuration of the microcontroller board 1. Install the board package distributed by Leafony STM32. Open File → Preferences and add the following to Additional Boards Manager URLs . ^2 https://github.com/Leafony/BoardManagerFiles/raw/master/Leafony_STM32_v3/package_leafony_stm_index.json 2. Open Tools → Board → Boards Manager . 3. Search for Leafony and install it. Installation may take several minutes. The Leafony_STM32_v3 package distributes version 1.9.2-R00 (checked September 15, 2026). 4. Select Tools → Board → Leafony STM32 . 5. Select Tools → Board part number → Leafony STM32 MCU . The default clock is 80 MHz; a 16 MHz board option is also provided for lower-power operation. 6. Select the connected port under Tools → Serial Port . If no port is available, see Serial port not found. Checking the operation of the microcontroller board Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow Restore the demo. 1. Set the STM32 MCU program switch to Program , then press the reset switch . (/leaf/processor/ap03/ap03_tips.jpg) 2. Follow the temperature and humidity sensor example to upload the program. Uploading may take some time. A successful upload displays Start operation achieved successfully . If that message is absent, the program will not run correctly. ^3 3. When uploading finishes, return the program switch to Run . The LED turns off. 4. Press the reset switch to start the program. Check that temperature and humidity values appear. Specifying pins for a sketch With this Leafony board definition, specify pins by Name or Port. (/leaf/processor/ap03/ap03_pinassign.png) Installing libraries Install the libraries required by your example from Libraries and board definitions. Check the board package and Arduino Core version before selecting STM32RTC and STM32LowPower versions. The timer-interrupt library MsTimer2.h is for AVR MCU and cannot be used with STM32 MCU. Use HardwareTimer as described below. HardwareTimer See the HardwareTimer documentation for details. This is an example of initialization: c++ HardwareTimer timer2 = new HardwareTimer (TIM2); timer2->setOverflow(LOOP_INTERVAL, MICROSEC_FORMAT); // 125ms timer2->attachInterrupt(intTimer); timer2->resume(); Interrupt routine: c++ void intTimer(void) bInterval = true; ： ： When in doubt See the FAQ for troubleshooting. ^1 : Historical testing recorded Windows 64-bit with versions 2.12.0, 2.6.0, and 2.4.0. Version 2.5.0 did not work in that testing. ^2 : The Boards Manager URL changed when the package was updated from Leafony_STM32 to Leafony_STM32_v3 . See the Leafony board package README. ^3 : If uploading is attempted without setting the switch to Program, the IDE may still display Writing to the board is complete , while the output below contains Timeout error occured while waiting for acknowledgement . The program will not run correctly.

title: STM32 MCU: PlatformIO Setup
description: Set up PlatformIO for the AP03 STM32 MCU leaf and upload a program.
content: Introduction This guide follows the Japanese STM32 PlatformIO guide and uses VS Code with PlatformIO to build a program that prints Hello World once per second. STM32CubeProgrammer uploads it through a USB leaf. You do not need Arduino IDE or its board package for this workflow. Install the latest stable software from the official distribution sites. The STM32CubeProgrammer version pins in older instructions are no longer required for this workflow. Required items - STM32 MCU leaf (AP03 / STM32L452REI6) and a USB leaf - A data-capable USB cable - A Windows, macOS or Linux computer with an internet connection For Basic Kit 2, replace the assembled AVR MCU with the STM32 MCU leaf before programming. Install the tools 1. Install Visual Studio Code for your OS and CPU. 2. Open Extensions in VS Code, find PlatformIO IDE published by PlatformIO , and install it. Wait for its initial setup to finish and restart VS Code if requested. 3. Install STM32CubeProgrammer from ST. Locate its command-line executable; you will use its actual path in upload_command . PlatformIO Core and its serial monitor are included in the IDE extension. If prompted for Python, follow PlatformIO's Python installation instructions; Linux also requires python3-venv . See the PlatformIO IDE documentation for setup details. Python is prepared automatically on supported operating systems. Add Japanese Language Pack for Visual Studio Code if you want a Japanese interface, or Teleplot for graphs. OS STM32CubeProgrammer command-line tool --- --- Windows bin/STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe under the installation folder macOS Contents/Resources/bin/STM32_Programmer_CLI inside STM32CubeProgrammer.app Linux bin/STM32_Programmer.sh under the installation folder Use a local project path with simple ASCII characters, such as C:/PlatformIO/Projects on Windows. Open the command terminal through PlatformIO → Quick Access → Miscellaneous → PlatformIO Core CLI . To change the default folder for new projects, run the following with your actual path and restart VS Code: sh pio settings set projects_dir "C:/PlatformIO/Projects" This does not move existing projects. See the projects_dir documentation. Simple paths help avoid path-handling problems. User folders and OneDrive locations differ between computers, so check the actual destination before copying an example. On macOS and Linux, replace the quoted path with the absolute path to your chosen folder. Install the latest ST STM32 platform Install PlatformIO's ST STM32 ( ststm32 ) development platform. For AP03, use its built-in Leafony Systems AP03 board definition. Run this command in PlatformIO Core CLI. Omitting the version installs the latest stable release from PlatformIO Registry. sh pio pkg install --global --platform "platformio/ststm32" If ST STM32 is already installed, update it to the latest release with: sh pio pkg update --global --platform "platformio/ststm32" Packages required by the project, including the Arduino framework, are installed automatically during the first build. See pio pkg install , pio pkg update , and the ST STM32 releases for details. Quick start Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow Restore the demo. 1. Create the project 1. Create an empty folder named STM32_Hello_World_Pjt and open it with File → Open Folder in VS Code. 2. Create platformio.ini and a src folder in the project root, then create main.cpp inside src . Their contents are provided in the steps below. text STM32_Hello_World_Pjt/ ├── platformio.ini └── src/ └── main.cpp 2. Identify the serial port With USB disconnected, assemble the STM32 MCU and USB leaves as shown in the connection example. Connect the USB leaf to your computer, then run: sh pio device list The connected port disappears and reappears when you unplug and reconnect the cable. OS Example port --- --- Windows COM3 macOS /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXXXXXX Linux /dev/ttyUSB0 If no port appears, check the cable, leaf connections and USB driver. Refer to the FAQ. On Linux, also follow PlatformIO's serial port permissions instructions. 3. Configure platformio.ini The following example is for Windows on COM3 . Replace the port and executable path with those on your computer. ini env:leafony_ap03 platform = ststm32 board = leafony_ap03 framework = arduino upload_protocol = custom upload_port = COM3 upload_command = "C:/Program Files/STMicroelectronics/STM32Cube/STM32CubeProgrammer/bin/STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe" -c port=$UPLOAD_PORT br=115200 -w "$SOURCE" 0x08000000 -v monitor_port = $ this.upload_port monitor_speed = 115200 On macOS, replace upload_port and upload_command with the following, using the actual port name: ini upload_port = /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXXXXXX upload_command = "/Applications/STMicroelectronics/STM32Cube/STM32CubeProgrammer/STM32CubeProgrammer.app/Contents/Resources/bin/STM32_Programmer_CLI" -c port=$UPLOAD_PORT br=115200 -w "$SOURCE" 0x08000000 -v On Linux, use the absolute installation path and actual serial port. This example uses the account name user : ini upload_port = /dev/ttyUSB0 upload_command = "/home/user/STMicroelectronics/STM32Cube/STM32CubeProgrammer/bin/STM32_Programmer.sh" -c port=$UPLOAD_PORT br=115200 -w "$SOURCE" 0x08000000 -v Setting Purpose --- --- env:leafony_ap03 Names the build environment and output folder platform = ststm32 Uses ST STM32 without a version pin board = leafony_ap03 Selects the built-in Leafony Systems AP03 board definition; use lowercase framework = arduino Uses the Arduino framework supported by ST STM32 upload_protocol = custom Runs upload_command for uploads $UPLOAD_PORT , $SOURCE Substituted by PlatformIO with the port and firmware path 0x08000000 Flash start address -v Verifies the uploaded data monitor_port Serial monitor port; the upload port in this example monitor_speed Serial baud rate; must match Serial.begin() Leave $UPLOAD_PORT and $SOURCE unchanged. See the PlatformIO upload command reference and STM32CubeProgrammer CLI manual. 4. Write the program Save the following as src/main.cpp : cpp include void setup() Serial.begin(115200); void loop() Serial.println("Hello World"); delay(1000); 5. Build Run PlatformIO → PROJECT TASKS → leafony_ap03 → General → Build , or run this command in the project folder: sh pio run -e leafony_ap03 The first build downloads the compiler and framework and can take several minutes. Check for SUCCESS at the end of the log and the generated file .pio/build/leafony_ap03/firmware.bin . If the project is not recognized, reopen the folder containing platformio.ini . If several projects or build environments are open, check that the selected target is leafony_ap03 in STM32_Hello_World_Pjt . 6. Upload to the STM32 MCU 1. Close any application using the serial port, including the serial monitor and Teleplot. Press Ctrl+C in PlatformIO's monitor terminal to stop it. 2. Set the STM32 MCU switch to Program and check that its LED is on. 3. Press Reset to enter programming mode. 4. Run PROJECT TASKS → leafony_ap03 → General → Upload , or: sh pio run -e leafony_ap03 -t upload Check the STM32CubeProgrammer log for successful connection, programming and verification. A verification success message may read Download verified successfully ; wording depends on the tool version. If there is a timeout or verification error, close other port users, reset in Program mode and upload again, even if the overall log says SUCCESS . 7. Check Hello World 1. Set the switch back to Run and check that the LED turns off. 2. Press Reset to start the program. 3. Run PROJECT TASKS → leafony_ap03 → General → Monitor , or: sh pio device monitor -e leafony_ap03 The following output should appear once per second: text Hello World Hello World Hello World Use an existing sample Download a project from the Leafony STM32 PlatformIO samples. Open the individual folder containing its platformio.ini , rather than the entire repository. Use the same platform, board and upload settings as in the quick start. For example, when using STM32_Hello_World_Pjt, set platform = ststm32 , board = leafony_ap03 and framework = arduino in platformio.ini , then configure the upload tool and port as described above. Review and preserve sample-specific lib_deps and build_flags . Replace old upload commands referencing Arduino15/.../STM32Tools/1.4.0/... with the path to your installed STM32CubeProgrammer. To update an existing project's ST STM32 platform to the latest release, replace a version constraint such as platform = ststm32@... with platform = ststm32 . Review library compatibility and adjust library version constraints as needed, then run the following in the project folder: sh pio pkg update Dependencies are updated within the version constraints in platformio.ini ; see the pio pkg update reference. Libraries Add libraries to lib_deps inside the env:... section you use. The Hello World example needs no additional libraries. If lib_deps already exists, append to its list. Add only the libraries needed for the leaves and functions you use. ini lib_deps = adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor adafruit/Adafruit BusIO https://github.com/Leafony/TBGLib Git URLs require Git. Restart VS Code after installing it and check that git --version works in the terminal. See Libraries and board definitions for the source catalog. Check STM32 Core and library compatibility below. Library versions in older samples ST STM32 20.0.0 moved to STM32 Arduino Core 3.0.0. Follow the STM32RTC requirements and STM32LowPower requirements: use the 2.x library lines with Core 3.x, and 1.x with Core 2.x. ini ; For STM32 Arduino Core 3.x lib_deps = stm32duino/STM32duino RTC@^2.0.0 stm32duino/STM32duino Low Power@^2.0.0 Check the framework-arduinoststm32 entry under PACKAGES in the build log to identify your Core. Do not use the AVR MsTimer2 library on STM32; use HardwareTimer instead. Even if an older sample specifies a version such as @1.2.0 , check each library's README against the Arduino Core used by your project. Serial plotter Install Teleplot for VSCode. Upload this example, return the switch to Run and reset: cpp include void setup() Serial.begin(115200); void loop() Serial.print(">seconds:"); Serial.println(millis() / 1000.0f); delay(100); Close PlatformIO's serial monitor. From the VS Code command palette run teleplot: Start teleplot session , choose the serial port and baud rate 115200 , then click Open . Check that seconds appears in the graph. Teleplot uses newline-terminated >name:value messages. Serial.println() supplies the newline. Close Teleplot's port before uploading another program. See also the STM32 Teleplot example. Port an Arduino IDE sketch src/main.cpp follows normal C++ rules. Add include , declare functions before use, and add required libraries to lib_deps . cpp include void printMessage(); void setup() Serial.begin(115200); printMessage(); void loop() void printMessage() Serial.println("Hello World"); Upload with the STM32CubeProgrammer GUI 1. Build and locate .pio/build/leafony_ap03/firmware.bin . If you renamed the environment, use its folder name instead. 2. Close other serial port users, switch to Program and press Reset. 3. Open STM32CubeProgrammer and connect using the following settings. Setting Value --- --- Connection UART Port The STM32 MCU serial port Baud rate 115200 Parity Even Data bits 8 Stop bits 1 Flow control OFF 4. Open Erasing & Programming . Select firmware.bin and start address 0x08000000 . 5. Enable Verify programming , click Start Programming , and check that verification succeeds. 6. Click Disconnect , return the switch to Run, press Reset, and check output in PlatformIO's serial monitor. Troubleshooting Symptom Check --- --- UnknownBoard or missing variant files Use lowercase board = leafony_ap03 and update ST STM32 to the latest release pio command not found Reopen the PlatformIO Core CLI terminal Upload tool not found Actual installation path and quotes around paths containing spaces Cannot open the port Port name, other applications holding the port, and Linux permissions Connection times out Program switch, Reset before upload, USB cable and port name No output after upload Switch back to Run, Reset, and monitor_port Garbled serial output Match monitor_speed to Serial.begin() ; this example uses 115200

title: STM32 MCU: STM32CubeIDE Setup
description: Build an AP03 STM32 Hello World project, upload it over UART and check serial output.
content: Introduction Use the Eclipse-based STM32CubeIDE to build a program for AP03 / STM32L452REI6 , upload it using STM32CubeProgrammer, and display Hello World every second over a serial connection. For a first Arduino sketch, use the Arduino IDE or PlatformIO guide instead. The original screenshots and workspace names use STM32CubeIDE 1.11.2. From version 2.0.0, STM32CubeMX is a separate tool : configure peripherals and generate the project there, then open it in STM32CubeIDE. See ST's release announcement. Use the branch below that matches your tools. What to prepare - AP03 STM32 MCU, a USB leaf, and a data-capable USB cable (swap the AVR MCU if using Basic Kit 2) - A computer supported by the tools below - STM32CubeIDE, STM32CubeMX for project generation, and STM32CubeProgrammer - A serial terminal such as Tera Term on Windows Preparation Install the STM32CubeIDE Download the Eclipse-based edition from the ST product page and follow the installer for your OS. Install STM32CubeMX separately for the 2.x workflow. Use the installation requirements for the version you selected. Install STM32CubeProgrammer Install STM32CubeProgrammer for UART uploads through the USB leaf. Install a serial terminal For Windows, obtain Tera Term from the official project. On macOS or Linux, use a serial terminal that can select the connected port and a baud rate of 115200. Quick start You can start from the existing Hello_World project using Import a project, or generate your own project as follows. Create a project 1. For CubeIDE 2.x: open STM32CubeMX and create a project for MCU STM32L452REI6 . For the original 1.x integrated UI: choose File → New → STM32 Project , use MCU/MPU Selector , enter STM32L452REI6 in Commercial Part Number , then select the device. 2. Name the project Hello_World and choose a local folder. With separate CubeMX, select STM32CubeIDE as the toolchain. With the original integrated wizard, the example used C++, Executable and STM32Cube. 3. Continue with peripheral settings below. Generate the project from CubeMX or the integrated UI, then open it in STM32CubeIDE. Configure the device and generate initialization code 1. In Pinout & Configuration , assign PA2 to USART2_TX and PA3 to USART2_RX . 2. Open Connectivity → USART2 , choose Asynchronous , disable hardware flow control, and set the baud rate to 115200 . 3. Generate code and open the generated main.c . Locate it in the project tree; source and build-output folders serve different purposes. Add the code Add code in the matching USER CODE blocks so you can identify it when regenerating code. Line numbers depend on the tool version and generated configuration. Include the standard I/O header: c / USER CODE BEGIN Includes / include / USER CODE END Includes / Before calling printf , disable output buffering: c / USER CODE BEGIN 1 / setbuf(stdout, NULL); / USER CODE END 1 / Inside the generated main loop, print once per second: c / USER CODE BEGIN 3 / printf("Hello World\r\n"); HAL_Delay(1000); Add _write to send printf output through USART2: c / USER CODE BEGIN 4 / int _write(int file, char ptr, int len) HAL_UART_Transmit(&huart2, (uint8_t )ptr, len, 10); return len; / USER CODE END 4 / Choose Project → Build All . Fix any build errors and locate the generated Hello_World.elf in the active build output folder, commonly Debug . Use the actual filename and path from your project. Upload with STM32CubeProgrammer Uploading replaces the program on the MCU. See Restore the demo if you want to run the kit demo again later. 1. Connect the USB leaf as shown in Connect to PC. Set AP03's program switch to Program , then press Reset . 2. Open STM32CubeProgrammer and choose UART . Select the connected port, baud rate 115200 , even parity, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit and no flow control, then select Connect . 3. In Erasing & Programming , select your generated .elf and enable Verify programming . 4. Select Start Programming and check for Download verified successfully . A completed build alone does not confirm an upload. 5. Disconnect STM32CubeProgrammer, return the AP03 switch to Run , then press Reset . Check serial output 1. Open the serial terminal and select the same port. Close other applications that hold the port. 2. Set it to 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit and no flow control. 3. Check that Hello World appears once per second. If it does not, check the Run switch, Reset, selected port and baud rate. Tips Import a project 1. Start STM32CubeIDE and choose your workspace. 2. Use File → Open Projects from File System (the menu may also mention archives) to select the downloaded project folder, then finish importing. 3. Open Window → Show View → Project Explorer if the project list is hidden. 4. Build the imported project, then use the upload procedure above. If migration is requested, retain a copy of the original project and review changes before rebuilding. For debugging instead of UART uploads, see Connecting the debugger.

title: How to run an example
description: Choose the right Leafony hardware, development tool, and source files, then check the build, upload, and execution results in order.
content: Match the leaf configuration and development tool, then check the build → upload → execution result in order . This makes it easier to find where a problem starts. Choose a purpose or CPU from the example catalog and check the required items in the article. 1. Match your hardware - Check the processor model number . Even examples using the same temperature and humidity sensor need different board selections and upload procedures for AVR, STM32, and ESP32. - Gather the leaves and additional parts . Check the model numbers, power supply, antenna, SIM, and other requirements in the article, as well as the kit name. Turn off the power before assembling, attaching, or removing leaves. - Choose the development tool . Open Arduino IDE sketches, PlatformIO projects, and STM32CubeIDE projects using their respective procedures. Start with your CPU under Development environment. 2. Obtain the source and libraries Use the article's source link to obtain all files required by the example. A sample with multiple files needs its headers and configuration files as well as the main .ino or main.cpp . Development tool What to open and check --- --- Arduino IDE The sketch folder and .ino file. Install the libraries and board package specified in the article PlatformIO The project folder containing platformio.ini . Check board , lib_deps , and the upload destination STM32CubeIDE The project folder containing .project and .cproject . Obtain Core , Drivers , and the other project files together GitHub links to main or master can change as the source is updated. Use a complete set from the same revision instead of mixing old and new files. Keep a copy of a previously working project before updating it so you can compare the changes. Libraries with similar names may be different implementations. Use the source specified in the article and check its CPU and Arduino Core requirements. For STM32, for example, see RTC and low-power library compatibility with the Core. 3. Check three stages Stage Success check If it stops here --- --- --- Build Compilation completes without errors Read the first error and check the board, CPU, and required libraries Upload The development tool reports a successful upload Check the USB cable, port, power supply, and program switch Execution You obtain the LED pattern, serial output, received data, or other result described in the article Check the switch to run mode, reset, wiring, and communication destination A successful build or upload is a separate check from successful operation. For communication examples, check the receiver or saved data as well as the transmitter log. Sensor values depend on the surroundings: check that readings are obtained and respond to changes, rather than expecting the same numbers as the screenshot. 4. If it does not work Start with the article's troubleshooting section and the FAQ. When contacting support, include the leaves, development tool, sample URL, stage reached, and first error. Do not send passwords, tokens, or SIM identifiers. In the catalog, Upcoming examples are not yet published. Previous versions & reference may use different procedures or conditions from current examples. Read any notices about discontinued external services before using them.
