title: KiCad Template Project
description: How to register the template, configure libraries, and start designing a Leafony expansion leaf with KiCad 10.0.x
content: Overview The Leafony template for KiCad lets you start designing an expansion leaf with the Leafony bus contacts and board outline already configured. It includes a schematic, PCB, dedicated symbol and footprint libraries, layer configuration, and design rules. The setup and usage instructions on this page are based on the KiCad template README on GitHub (Japanese). Development environment - KiCad 10.0.x - KiCad's standard symbol and footprint libraries :::caution Supported version The included schematics, PCB, and footprints are saved in KiCad 10.0 format. The previous requirement of “KiCad 5.0.0 or later” does not apply to the current files. KiCad 9 and earlier are not supported. ::: When starting KiCad for the first time, choose the option to use its standard libraries. If your system provides the libraries as separate packages, as on some Linux distributions, install those packages as well. Power symbols in the schematic use the standard power library. Download On GitHub - leafony/cad-template, select Code → Download ZIP and extract the archive. If you use Git, you can download the repository with this command: sh git clone https://github.com/leafony/cad-template.git Download the entire folder, since the project also needs its libraries and other referenced files. In the paths below, replace cad-template with the actual folder where you cloned the repository or extracted the ZIP archive. Main files The following files and folders are inside cad-template/KiCad/Leafony_Template/ . Path Purpose --- --- Leafony_Template.kicad_pro Project settings, design rules, and net classes Leafony_Template.kicad_sch Schematic with the Leafony bus, power connections, and signal labels Leafony_Template.kicad_pcb PCB with the board outline, contacts, vias, and copper zone keepouts lib/Leafony.kicad_sym Leafony Bus symbol lib/Leafony.pretty/ CN_F29_B29 footprint sym-lib-table Project-specific symbol library table; empty as distributed fp-lib-table Project-specific footprint library table; Leafony is already registered meta/ Template name, description, icon, and preview image Register lib/Leafony.kicad_sym as the symbol library, rather than the legacy files leafony_template-cache.lib , lib/Leafony.dcm , or lib/Leafony.bak . The .kicad_prl and fp-info-cache files contain personal settings and cached data; they are not libraries to register. Usage Register the user template 1. Launch the KiCad project manager. 2. Open Preferences → Configure Paths… . Menu names may vary with your OS and display language. 3. Set KICAD_USER_TEMPLATE_DIR to the absolute path of the KiCad folder in the downloaded repository. 4. Save the settings. If the template does not appear in the list, restart KiCad. OS Example setting --- --- Windows C:/Users/your-name/Documents/cad-template/KiCad macOS /Users/your-name/Documents/cad-template/KiCad Linux /home/your-name/cad-template/KiCad This variable must point to the parent folder containing Leafony_Template . Check that Leafony_Template/meta/info.html exists under the configured folder. If you already use another user template folder, you can keep that setting and copy the entire Leafony_Template folder into it. Create a new project 1. In the project manager, select File → New Project… . 2. Select Leafony Leaf from the template list. Filter the list to user templates if needed. 3. Click OK , then choose a working folder and a new project name, such as my_leaf . 4. Open the generated my_leaf.kicad_pro , then launch the schematic and PCB editors from the project manager. The template files are copied into the new project, and the main files are renamed to match the project name. The lib folder and library tables are also copied. Save the new project in a different location from the original template folder. To inspect the template, you can open Leafony_Template/Leafony_Template.kicad_pro directly. To design your own leaf, edit the newly created project. Configure the symbol library The template's sym-lib-table , copied into the new project, is empty as distributed. Placed symbols are also stored in the schematic, but you must register the library to add or reference symbols from it. 1. Open the schematic editor from the project manager. 2. Open Preferences → Manage Symbol Libraries… . 3. Select Project Specific Libraries . 4. Use the option to add an existing library and select lib/Leafony.kicad_sym inside your new project. 5. Set the entries to the following values, enable the library, and save. Field Value --- --- Nickname Leafony Library path $ KIPRJMOD /lib/Leafony.kicad_sym Library format KiCad $ KIPRJMOD is the current project folder, set automatically by KiCad. You do not need to add or change it in the path settings. Check that Leafony:Leafony Bus appears in the symbol chooser. If you are using the existing CN1 , you do not need to place another symbol just to check the library. Check the footprint library The footprint library is already registered in fp-lib-table , so no additional setup is normally needed. In the PCB editor, open Preferences → Manage Footprint Libraries… and check the project-specific libraries. Field Value --- --- Nickname Leafony Library path $ KIPRJMOD /lib/Leafony.pretty Library format KiCad The library is configured correctly if Leafony:CN_F29_B29 appears. If you register it again, select the Leafony.pretty folder, not an individual .kicad_mod file. When moving or sharing the project with another PC, copy the entire project, including the lib folder and library tables, to preserve the relative references using $ KIPRJMOD . Start designing Template defaults The values below are the settings in the included files. Check the layer configuration, manufacturing constraints, and net classes in Board Setup , and compare them with your manufacturer's requirements. Item Default value --- --- Board outline Maximum Edge.Cuts dimensions: 23 × 20 mm. The connector side is 20 mm wide, with extensions on both sides of the board Copper layers 4 layers: F.Cu / In1.Cu / In2.Cu / B.Cu Board thickness 0.8 mm Bus contacts CN1 , with 29 contacts on each side ( F1 – F29 and B1 – B29 ) Mounting holes Two non-plated holes, 2.05 mm in diameter Minimum track width and minimum clearance 0.1016 mm Track width for the Default net class 0.127 mm Via diameter / drill diameter for the Default net class 0.56 mm / 0.30 mm Copper zone keepouts are configured around the connector. Use the PCB data as the reference for the actual board outline, contact positions, and hole positions. Edit the schematic and PCB 1. Check the pin assignments of the leaves you will use, then add components and wiring to the schematic. Verify the Leafony bus contact numbers and existing signal names as you connect them. 2. Assign footprints to the added components and run the schematic's electrical rules check (ERC). 3. Select Tools → Update PCB from Schematic… to apply the changes to the PCB. 4. Check the contact and mounting hole positions, as well as possible component interference with other leaves, then place the components and route the board. 5. Refill the copper zones and run the design rules check (DRC) to check for unconnected items and manufacturing rule violations. 6. Export the Gerber and drill files, and check them against your manufacturer's requirements. See the Custom Leaf Development resources for pin assignments and I2C addresses. Troubleshooting Symptom What to check --- --- Leafony Leaf does not appear in the template list Check that KICAD_USER_TEMPLATE_DIR points to the parent folder of Leafony_Template , with Leafony_Template/meta/info.html underneath it. Reopen the list or restart KiCad. KiCad reports that the file format is too new Check that you are opening the files with KiCad 10.0.x. The Leafony symbol library cannot be found Register Leafony in the new project's symbol library table. It is not registered in the distributed table. Leafony:CN_F29_B29 cannot be found Check that the project contains lib/Leafony.pretty and fp-lib-table , and that the nickname and path match the settings above. Standard symbols such as power cannot be found Check that KiCad's standard libraries are installed and enabled in the global library table. Libraries cannot be found after moving to another PC Copy the lib folder as well, and check that library paths use $ KIPRJMOD instead of absolute paths from the original PC. title: Pin Assignment Editor
description: Create Leafony pin assignment diagrams and tables comparing pin usage across leaves, then download them as PNG or SVG images.
content: Create a pin assignment diagram for one leaf or a table comparing pin usage across multiple leaves. Edit the port names and signals, then download your diagram as a PNG or SVG image. How to use 1. Choose a leaf or add a blank leaf. You can compare up to eight leaves. 2. Edit the leaf name and each pin's port name, signal name, and category. Switch between "Single leaf" and "Leaf comparison" to check the result. 3. Save the image as PNG or SVG. To continue editing later, save your editing data as JSON. Your edits are saved automatically in your current browser. To continue on another device, load the JSON file you saved. This tool draws the pin information you enter. It does not automatically determine whether leaves can be connected together. When designing a circuit, check pin voltages and connection requirements in the technical documentation for each leaf.

title: Privacy and analytics
description: How Leafony documentation uses Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity.
content: This site uses Google Analytics to understand site traffic and improve its documentation. Google Analytics uses cookies and similar technologies to collect information about pages viewed, referring pages, browsers and devices, and interactions such as scrolling and link clicks. This information is sent to Google. We use the resulting reports to understand visitor numbers, popular pages, and traffic sources. For information about how Google handles this data, see the Google Privacy Policy and How Google uses information from sites or apps that use our services. To disable the use of data by Google Analytics, you can install the Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on in a supported browser. See the linked page for compatibility and setup instructions. Microsoft Clarity We use Microsoft Clarity to improve the readability and usability of these docs. On eligible pages, measurement starts without cookies by default. Page visits, clicks, scrolling, and browser and device information are sent to Microsoft and help us understand usage through heatmaps and similar reports. Without cookies, we cannot connect activity across pages or recognize returning visitors as part of the same journey. Use “Analytics settings” at the bottom of each page to choose “Measure without cookies”, “Allow cookies for analytics”, or “Stop collection”. Allowing cookies enables Clarity cookies for session recordings and journeys across pages. “Stop collection” stops further Clarity collection; it does not delete information already sent. Your choice is saved in this browser and can be changed at any time. Set it separately on other browsers or devices. Previously saved choices to stop collection remain in effect. We apply strict masking to text and inputs. Clarity does not load on contact, question-form, or privacy pages, or URLs containing query parameters. Recording stops on the current page when you start using an input, such as search. Clarity also stays off when your browser enables Do Not Track (DNT) or Global Privacy Control (GPC), or when your settings cannot be saved or read. Microsoft processes the information it receives to provide Clarity and for purposes such as improving its products and services, in accordance with its privacy statement and Clarity terms. We always send advertising consent as denied, disabling data sharing from Clarity to Microsoft Ads. This setting does not stop all processing by Microsoft, including providing and improving Clarity. For more information, see the Microsoft Privacy Statement and Clarity Terms of Use. These settings apply to Clarity. For Google Analytics settings, see the section above. Information collected through the question form We use your email address, question, tried steps, hardware and development environment, publication preference, and consent record to review and answer questions and improve support. Submissions are stored on an access-restricted server and are not published automatically. We retain them only for as long as needed for handling and administration. Even with publication permission, we remove email addresses and personal or confidential information before staff review and edit the question and answer for publication. Questions marked for private replies only are not published. To handle your question, we share its title, text, reply email address, hardware and development environment, tried steps, reference number, and publication preference in a private Slack channel accessible only to support staff. Sharing within the support team is separate from permission to publish in the public Q&A. Questions marked for private replies only are still shared with support staff, but are not published publicly. For questions submitted under the earlier notice that excluded text and contact details from Slack, we keep that handling unchanged. We use Cloudflare Turnstile to prevent spam; Cloudflare processes browser and connection information. See Cloudflare’s privacy policy. The intake service does not store raw IP addresses; it uses short-lived derived values for submission rate limits. Google Analytics and Clarity do not load on the question form. title: Terms
description: Understand terms used in Leafony documentation: BLE, I2C, SPI and UART communication; MCU, MEMS and PWM; leaves, the Leafony bus and related organizations.
content: Alphabetical order BLE Bluetooth Low Energy is a wireless communication technology designed for low-power data transfer. Leafony uses it, for example, to send sensor readings to a compatible smartphone or computer. Both the device and the application need to support the connection. See the Bluetooth SIG technology overview for more information. DC DC stands for Direct Current, in which current flows in one direction. A DC motor operates from a DC power supply. The AIx1 Motor leaf uses a motor supply and a motor driver to control motors in response to MCU signals. I2C I2C stands for Inter-Integrated Circuit and is pronounced "I-squared-C" or "I-two-C." It is a communication interface that connects a microcontroller to sensors and other devices. Devices share two signal lines, SDA for data and SCL for timing, and addresses identify the communication partner. Power and ground connections are also required. See the I2C address map for Leafony addresses and the NXP I2C-bus specification for details. IoT/CPS IoT stands for Internet of Things and CPS stands for Cyber-Physical Systems. CPS refers to systems that connect physical and digital spaces. Jumper pin A small part placed over adjacent pins to connect them electrically, also called a shunt or shorting jumper. It is often used to change a board setting. It is different from a jumper wire, which connects terminals using a wire. Jumper wire A wire used to connect terminals, often for prototyping with breadboards or pin headers. Male ends plug into sockets, while female ends fit over pins. Choose the combination that matches the terminals you are connecting. LCD LCD stands for Liquid Crystal Display, a type of screen used to display text, numbers, or images. Leafony's AI04 LCD is a character display with two rows of eight characters. Leaf A leaf is an electronic board or module, typically about 2 cm square, that forms the basis of Leafony. It is called a leaf because it is small and green. More precisely, a leaf is an electronic board that has a Leafony bus. You can easily create your own original leaves and sell them commercially by labeling them "Leafony compliant." Leafony or the Leafony platform Leafony is an open hardware and software platform built by combining leaves. Its very small size and low power consumption make it suitable for prototyping IoT/CPS systems and improving development efficiency. Leafony also works in the Arduino environment, so you can use the many software resources available online. You can also develop software in environments other than Arduino. Leafony is a word coined from Leaf and Symphony. It expresses the hope that individual leaves will come together to create new value, just as the sounds of different instruments combine to make music. Leafony technical information is generally free to use, including for commercial purposes. See the License section for details. Companies and individuals sell their own leaves labeled "Leafony compliant," and such activities are encouraged. However, Leafony is a registered trademark, so please refrain from including Leafony in product names to avoid market confusion. Leafony block It is an electronic device that is made up of multiple leaves. Normally, stacked leaves form a block, so it is called a leaf block. An electronic device made by combining leaves, even if the structure is flat and spread out, is called a leaf block. Leafony bus A common pathway that connects multiple leaves to each other is called a Leafony bus. Its electrical and physical specifications define the signal and power connections. It typically occupies a 20 mm x 5.5 mm area on a leaf. A Leafony bus-compliant leaf can communicate with other leaves, but whether it works with the Leafony platform without problems also depends on the software and other factors. Leafony bus compliance therefore indicates connectivity close to the physical level. The Leafony bus artwork is copyrighted and published under the CC-BY License . You may use it free of charge, including commercially, by stating "Leafony compliant." You are therefore free to develop and sell your own leaves. However, Leafony is a registered trademark, so do not label the leaves you make with Leafony itself. A leaf bearing the Leafony label indicates that its product quality has been verified. Leafony connector A connector newly developed to interconnect leaves using anisotropic conductive rubber. It serves as both a male and female connector. Leaves can also be connected using techniques such as solder-based thermocompression bonding, but using a Leafony connector is simpler. LEAFONY SYSTEMS Co., Ltd. LEAFONY SYSTEMS was the company that manufactured and sold Leafony products with the registered Leafony trademark, based on the research and development by the Trillion Node Engine Project. Leaves bearing the Leafony label had their interoperability verified by the project. In March 2026, LEAFONY SYSTEMS transferred its entire business to MITDIR Inc. MITDIR Inc. MITDIR Inc. acquired the entire business of LEAFONY SYSTEMS Co., Ltd. in March 2026 and currently handles the sales and support of Leafony products. By combining Leafony with its existing IoT and AI technologies, MITDIR works to provide DX solutions and promote IoT technology through collaboration with the research community. Leafony bus-compliant leaves are also sold by other companies and individuals under the "Leafony compliant" label, and such activities are encouraged. However, Leafony is not included in those product names. MCU MCU stands for Microcontroller Unit. It is an IC that runs programs to read sensors and control outputs such as LEDs or motors. It includes a CPU, memory, and input/output functions. A Leafony board carrying an MCU is called an MCU leaf. MEMS MEMS stands for Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems. The term refers to technology and devices that use tiny mechanical structures and electronic circuits. A MEMS microphone converts the movement of a tiny membrane caused by sound into an electrical signal. AI03 MIC&VR&LED includes a MEMS microphone. PWM PWM stands for Pulse Width Modulation. A signal switches on and off at a regular interval, while the proportion of time spent on is varied. It can be used to adjust LED brightness or motor output through a motor driver. The proportion of on-time is called the duty cycle. SPI SPI stands for Serial Peripheral Interface. It transfers data between a microcontroller and peripheral devices in time with a clock signal. Leafony uses SPI for devices such as microSD cards. Check each leaf's specifications for the signals used to select a device and the pin assignments. Trillion-node engine The electronics platform developed by the Trillion Node Engine Project. Hardware and software whose research and development has been completed are organized and released to the public under the name Leafony. Trillion-node engine project The Trillion Node Engine Project is a research and development project commissioned and subsidized by the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO). Trillion-node study-group Many IT nodes, including IoT/CPS systems, are expected to be used throughout society in the future. The Trillion-node study-group discusses that future and shares information. It uses Leafony as a practical basis for these discussions and works to promote its use to support the development of IoT/CPS. It also provides a place to connect related companies with needs and technologies to offer. UART UART stands for Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter. It provides serial communication using TX to transmit and RX to receive data. Both devices need matching settings such as the communication speed. Leafony uses UART between MCU and communication leaves, and for communication with a computer through a USB-to-UART leaf. Harness Electrical connections between a Leafony block and the outside world may require wiring. Such wiring is called a harness.
